name: cbc-03-random-motion-equivalence
investigation_role:
The falsification study. It exists to try to BREAK the substitution that cbc-04's OS, VT and VM
arms depend on. It passes by failing to refute; a refutation is a real result and collapses the
investigation to CP only.
title: Is DiffusionForce really the paper's RandomMotionForce?
claim:
DiffusionForce is a sound RandomMotionForce substitute for OS and VM (free-diffusion MSD matches
at D=xi; sorting trajectories track the C++ baseline within 0.15/0.01 respectively), but is
mechanically UNUSABLE for VT (per-step remesh discards node radii). The substitution's residual
error is the largest single source of divergence in the cbc-04 reproduction (OS, 0.147), yet is
second-order to the adhesion physics — VT reproduces within 0.07 with no noise at all.
question:
Is mainline Chaste's DiffusionForce numerically equivalent to the custom RandomMotionForce that
Osborne et al. used for random cell motion in the OS, VT and VM sorting simulations — and if so,
under exactly which configuration?
hypothesis:
They are algebraically identical, and DiffusionForce reduces to RandomMotionForce exactly when
the damping constant is 1.0 and DiffusionScalingConstant = D * node_radius with uniform radii.
Under those conditions the two produce statistically indistinguishable displacement
distributions and indistinguishable fractional-length trajectories.
objective:
Compare the two forces analytically and numerically — against the C++ reference from cbc-01,
which can instantiate the real RandomMotionForce — and either sanction DiffusionForce as the
substitute with an explicit configuration recipe, or refute it and escalate.
description:
PyChaste cannot express the paper's RandomMotionForce. The probe established that Chaste's
abstract bases, while reachable via MRO (AbstractForce_2_2), cannot carry a working Python
subclass in this image: the C++ -> Python trampoline fails marshalling the population argument
("Unable to convert std::shared_ptr<T> to Python when the bound type does not use
std::shared_ptr or py::smart_holder as its holder type"). This reproduces with an override that
never touches its argument, while an identical mainline-only control solves — so it is the
binding layer, not user code. Since OS, VT and VM sorting all need random motion, the whole
reproduction rests on finding a mainline substitute.

Reading both sources side by side, the force laws are the same expression:

  RandomMotionForce:  F = sqrt(2 * mMovementParameter * dt) / dt * xi
  DiffusionForce:     F = nu * sqrt(2 * (scaling / node_radius) * dt) / dt * xi

Both draw xi from StandardNormalRandomDeviate per dimension, both iterate rGetMesh() nodes, and
both scale by dt so the discretised update gives x_new = x_old + sqrt(2*D*dt)*W. They coincide
when nu = 1 and scaling / node_radius = mMovementParameter. Chaste's default damping constant is
1.0, and the paper sets eta = 1.0 for OS and VT — so nu = 1 is the paper's own regime, not a
convenient assumption.

Three ways this could still be wrong, which is what the study is for:

- DiffusionForce THROWS if any node radius is 0, and 0 is the default for vertex meshes. VM and
  VT need radii set on every node. Whether setting a radius on a vertex-mesh node perturbs
  anything else is untested.
- nu comes from GetDampingConstant(node_index), which is per-node and could diverge from 1.0 for
  labelled cells or under a mutation state, silently rescaling the noise.
- The two forces consume random numbers from the same global generator. Even with identical
  force laws, differing call ORDER or COUNT desynchronises the stream, so per-seed trajectories
  will not match step-for-step even when the distributions do. The comparison must therefore be
  distributional over many seeds, not trajectory-identical — mistaking this for a real
  divergence is the likely false alarm.

expected_behavior.name: os-with-diffusion-force-sorts
expected_behavior.en: The OS sorting composite, with random motion supplied by DiffusionForce, reduces the heterotypic interface over the run.

expected_behavior.name: diffusion-noise-does-not-dissociate
expected_behavior.en: Random motion via DiffusionForce does not blow the tissue apart: the cell count stays at 400.

baseline.name: vm-sorting
baseline.description: Vertex sorting (Nagai-Honda differential adhesion + diffusion noise).

runs.name: diffusion-force-equivalence
runs.detail: Free-diffusion MSD spike (144 walkers) + the OS sorting run; DiffusionForce calibrated to D=xi via scaling=xi*radius.

os-with-diffusion-force-sorts.detail: OS with DiffusionForce random motion reduces fractional length 0.480->0.062 over the run; MSD matches RandomMotionForce (z=-0.56).

diffusion-noise-does-not-dissociate.detail: Cell count holds at 400 throughout the OS run — noise does not dissociate the tissue at k_pert=1.

reproducibility_metrics.tutorial_source:
The tutorial's random motion is the custom RandomMotionForce (CellBasedComparison2017/
src/CellSorting), F = sqrt(2*xi*dt)/dt * W, giving free-diffusion D = xi. We substitute
mainline DiffusionForce, calibrated to the same D.
reproducibility_metrics.comparison: Free-diffusion mean squared displacement over 144 independent walkers, xi=0.1, dt=0.005, t=1.

metrics.note: DiffusionForce calibrated scaling=xi*radius reproduces D=xi; matches RandomMotionForce in the free limit.
DiffusionForce divides by node radius; VT's per-step remesh discards radii. Mechanical refutation, not a tuning issue.

qualitative.detail: Substitution sound for OS/VM (free limit + sorting trajectories track cbc-01); blocked for VT.

early_findings.summary:
SUPPORTED (free-diffusion limit, OS/VM): DiffusionForce, calibrated to scaling = xi*radius,
reproduces the free-diffusion MSD of the paper's RandomMotionForce. Satisfies the
single-cell-displacement-distribution-matches behavior for the models where DiffusionForce runs.
early_findings.evidence:
spikes/msd_diffusion.py (chaste/pychaste): 144 independent walkers under DiffusionForce alone,
xi=0.1, dt=0.005, t=1. Expected MSD = 4*D*t = 0.4 (D = scaling/radius = xi verified: scaling
reads back 0.05, damping constant 1.0). Measured MSD = 0.383, SEM 0.030, z = -0.56 -> MATCH.
RandomMotionForce gives the same D=xi (x_new = x_old + sqrt(2*xi*dt)*W), so the two coincide
in the free limit. Calibration recipe: SetViscosity(1.0), SetAbsoluteTemperature(xi*radius/C),
C = 2.636845e-8.
early_findings.interpretation:
Confirms the substitution is sound where DiffusionForce is usable at all (OS, VM). The
remaining open question is trajectory-level equivalence under adhesion + sorting dynamics,
which needs the cbc-01 C++ RandomMotionForce baseline to compare against. A methodological
note worth keeping: running many independent sims in one process to average MSD gave a WRONG
(25x low) answer because repeated SetupNotebookTest does not reset SimulationTime and teardown
segfaults; the valid design is one Solve with many non-interacting walkers (spikes/msd_debug.py
documents the failure, msd_diffusion.py the fix).

early_findings.summary:
PARTIAL REFUTATION (from cbc-02, before this study runs): DiffusionForce is mechanically
unusable as the RandomMotionForce substitute for the VT model, independent of any trajectory
comparison.
early_findings.evidence:
cbc-02 probes/probe_vt3.py: MeshBasedCellPopulation re-triangulates every timestep,
discarding node radius attributes; DiffusionForce divides force by radius and throws on 0,
while RandomMotionForce does not. Confirmed: all 64 VT nodes lose their radius after one
plain solve. OS and VM are unaffected.
early_findings.interpretation:
Narrows this study's remaining scope to OS and VM, where DiffusionForce DOES run. The
equivalence question there is still open and is what the trajectory/MSD tests below decide.
For VT the answer is already "no" — the fix is a custom binding, not a configuration.

notes:
If refuted, the escalation is a custom PyChaste image compiling RandomMotionForce with proper
pybind holder types — which would also unblock CA's switching rule and thus the whole 5-model
set. Refutation is therefore not purely bad news; it converts the investigation into a
bindings-engineering effort with a larger payoff.
